title: Osie Johnson: bringing him to a record date and to New York
summary: Hinton and Jones recall bringing young Osie Johnson to a Billy Williams record date and Jones's coaching of him in Washington and New York.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I met him for the first time when you and I were on a record date together for the Billy Williams Quartet. You and I were making a record session and this kid was in town with Earl Hines and we thought he was a pretty nice kid. You liked him and you said, "Bring him along on the date." On this particular date at the end of that take he said, "Oh yeah!" Billy Williams said, "Keep that in."

And we handed him a withholding slip so he could get paid. He came with you on the date; you was to show him what New York was about, and he wound up being what New York is really about. What was his name?

You see, the thing of it is I had to go to Washington. I knew a little drummer by the name of Cees. So Tommy Potter and all the guys, John Malachi, all of the guys were going down to the Crystal Cavern. I'd go down there and hang around with them and sit down in a little restaurant, sit down and talk about things to come. I'd say, "Now you're going to grow up and when you come to New York, look me up. Go around and hang out with so-and-so and learn," because they had a couple of drummers around there, just doing their thing. They never went anywhere because you see it was enough; they had the experience.

That particular day he comes in. He says, "Well, old gal, I don't have no card. I said, "Well, I'm going to get you on and Monday night at the Birdland I've got these little vocalists around here and you can pick up these recording dates. I went to Morris Levy and Morris Levy got him his card, and boom, and fool around -

Osie Johnson. I said, "Now, old gal, you got the music, because I don't want no dumb drummers around me. You learn C and G; you going to know full chords; you going to know diminished chords." He said, "I don't know nothing about no drums." I said, "Come on, now." He kept fooling around and fooling around and when the thing come to a head - you remember, you and I had a thing we were going to go around and show somebody how to play with the rhythm section. I suggested to you, now there's no way in the world you can miss with all these violins and all this recording coming on. There's no way you can miss, you get your own rhythm section and they all walk in and you don't care what they play..." So you, Benny, Hank Jones, and Osie sat You know what happened to me. I as sitting with Old Gal, I was sitting with Crawford at the funeral and I was the last one, me and Tommy Potter. I put Osie to bed and Major Holley was going to go over and cut his hair. I said, "You won't cut his hair." He's doing all right. I said, "No, you won't cut his hair." I came into Beerstein But Charles Osie, just out of that one little incident when he turned
here and you didn't care what the other people played. You'd know what you were going to play. HINTON: We became the New York rhythm section.
